http://www.bgnes.com/society/ancient-gre.text: An ancient marble slab bearing a Greek inscription and depictions of three laurel wreaths is embedded in the floor of the narthex at Romania’s Dragomirna Monastery, Evenimentul Zilei reported. The monastery is located near Suceava in the historical region of Moldavia. The complex was built in the early 17th century at the initiative of Metropolitan Anastasie Crimca. The slab is not a recent archaeological discovery. Its inscription was first published in March 1885 in the Greek-language newspaper Hesperos, which was printed in Leipzig. Two years later, Romanian historian and epigrapher Grigore Tocilescu introduced the document to the academic community. The text is written in Ancient Greek and dates from the Hellenistic period. Researchers have variously dated it to the third century or the late second century BC, according to a study published in the academic journal Pontica. What Kind of Document Is It?The inscription is an honorary decree, known as a psephisma, granting the status of proxenos to the architect Epikrates, son of Nikoboulos of Byzantion. In ancient Greece, a proxenos was a citizen of one city-state who represented the interests of another city and its citizens. The institution shared certain similarities with modern consular functions but was not equivalent to a present-day consulate or honorary citizenship. The text indicates that Epikrates was hired to carry out public construction works. He was honoured for his services and granted the right of proxeny for himself and his descendants. The inscription uses the rare Greek word “telamon” to describe the stone stele. This does not mean the object was an architectural telamon in the modern sense of the term. Which City Issued the Decree?The name of the city that honoured the architect has not survived on the damaged slab. Over the years, scholars have linked the decree to several ancient cities, including Histria, Tomis, Callatis, Apollonia, Tyras and Olbia. Romanian historian D. M. Pippidi suggested that the document may have originated in Histria. A more recent analysis by historian Victor Cojocaru identifies the northwestern Black Sea city of Olbia as its most likely place of origin. Conclusive evidence is lacking, however, and the decree’s provenance remains the subject of scholarly debate. It is also unclear how the slab reached Dragomirna Monastery. It may first have been transported to Suceava through ecclesiastical or commercial links with cities around the Black Sea before being reused as building material. At the monastery, it was incorporated into the flooring and may have served as a grave cover. | BGNES
